summary: Psalm 54 opens with a heading that links the prayer to David and the Ziphites, then moves quickly into a plea for God to save and vindicate. The speaker names hostile people who seek his life, declares that God sustains him, asks God to deal with his enemies, and ends with promised sacrifice and thanks for deliverance.
whyItMatters: This short psalm shows a common Psalms movement from danger to trust to thanksgiving. It also shows how an individual crisis can become a preserved prayer for later worshiping communities.

context.author: The heading associates this psalm with David; Psalms as a book contains many writers and collections, and the exact force of Davidic headings is debated.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to the whole Psalter is misleading.
context.setting: Book II of Psalms, within a collection that includes David-associated prayers of distress and confidence. This psalm's heading names the Ziphites reporting David's hiding place to Saul.
context.literaryForm: A short Hebrew prayer poem with a heading, petition, complaint, confidence, appeal for judgment, and thanksgiving vow.

outline.heading: Heading and plea for rescue
outline.note: The psalm is introduced for musical use and connected with David's danger among the Ziphites; the prayer asks God to save and vindicate.

outline.heading: A request to be heard
outline.note: The speaker asks God to hear his prayer and listen to his words.

outline.heading: The threat named
outline.note: Strangers and violent men are described as seeking the speaker's life and disregarding God.

outline.heading: Trust in God's help
outline.note: The poem turns from threat to confidence: God is the helper and sustainer.

outline.heading: Appeal for judgment
outline.note: The speaker asks that evil return on his enemies and that God destroy them in truth.

outline.heading: Thanksgiving promised
outline.note: The psalm ends with a free will offering, thanks to Yahweh's name, and testimony that God has delivered the speaker from trouble.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. On stringed instruments. A contemplation by David, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul, “Isn’t David hiding himself among us?” Save me, God, by your name. Vindicate me in your might.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives both the heading's remembered crisis and the basic plea of the psalm: rescue and vindication from God.

keyVerses.text: For strangers have risen up against me. Violent men have sought after my soul. They haven’t set God before them. Selah.
keyVerses.why: This is the complaint that explains why the speaker is praying: hostile people threaten his life and act without regard for God.

keyVerses.text: Behold, God is my helper. The Lord is the one who sustains my soul.
keyVerses.why: The center of the psalm shifts from danger to trust, naming God as helper and sustainer.

keyVerses.text: With a free will offering, I will sacrifice to you. I will give thanks to your name, Yahweh, for it is good.
keyVerses.why: The ending looks toward worship and gratitude, not only escape from danger.

questions.question: What situation does the heading give for this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading connects the psalm with David, the Ziphites, and Saul. It says the Ziphites came to Saul and reported that David was hiding among them. The chapter itself then speaks as a prayer from someone under threat, asking God to save and vindicate him.

questions.question: Does the heading prove David wrote the psalm exactly as a modern author byline would?
questions.answer: The heading associates the psalm with David and with a remembered event involving the Ziphites and Saul. Davidic headings are ancient features of the Psalter, but their grammar may indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging. Readers differ on how much historical precision each heading gives, so the heading should be treated as important evidence without pretending it answers every question.

questions.question: What does the speaker ask God to do at the start?
questions.answer: The speaker asks God to save him by God's name and to vindicate him in God's might. In the next verse he asks God to hear and listen. The opening is direct petition rather than explanation or praise.

questions.question: Who are the enemies in this psalm?
questions.answer: Verse 3 calls them strangers and violent men who have sought after the speaker's soul. The heading names the Ziphites and Saul as the remembered setting, but the body of the poem speaks in broader poetic language. That broader wording lets the prayer move beyond one episode into a form later readers could voice in danger.

questions.question: What does “soul” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: The word “soul” appears in verses 3 and 4. In this psalm it names the speaker's threatened life or whole self: violent men seek it, and the Lord sustains it. The chapter does not pause to define the term, so it is safest to read it from the immediate contrast between mortal danger and divine support.

questions.question: Why does verse 5 ask God to destroy the enemies?
questions.answer: Verse 5 is an imprecatory line: the speaker asks God to repay evil and destroy the enemies in truth. The psalm voices the danger and anger of someone under threat, but it hands judgment to God rather than describing the speaker carrying it out. Readers may find the line morally difficult; the chapter presents it as prayer from distress, not as a direct permission for private revenge.

questions.question: What changes in verse 4?
questions.answer: Verse 4 turns from accusation and danger to confidence. The speaker says God is his helper and that the Lord sustains his soul. The trouble is not gone from the psalm, but the speaker's attention shifts toward the one he trusts to preserve him.

questions.question: What is a “free will offering” doing at the end of a danger prayer?
questions.answer: The speaker promises to sacrifice with a free will offering and to give thanks to Yahweh's name. The ending imagines rescue leading to worship, gratitude, and public acknowledgment. The psalm does not describe the ritual in detail, but it clearly connects deliverance with thanks.

questions.question: Has the rescue already happened by verse 7?
questions.answer: Verse 7 says God has delivered the speaker out of all trouble and that his eye has seen triumph over his enemies. Readers differ on whether this is spoken after rescue, or in confident anticipation as part of the prayer's movement. The chapter itself gives the statement as the closing reason for thanksgiving.

glossary.def: The heading directs the psalm for musical or worship use, though the exact ancient performance setting is not reconstructed here.
The heading says the psalm is for stringed instruments, marking it as a song or performed prayer.
A label in the heading for this kind of psalm; the chapter does not define the term further.
A preserved performance marker in verse 3. Its exact ancient function is uncertain, so it is best read as a signal within the poem rather than translated into a precise instruction.
The offering named in verse 6 as part of the speaker's promised thanksgiving to God.
